stem: A nurse is suctioning an adult client through an artificial airway. Which technique is consistent with current AARC guidance?

options.A: Apply suction while advancing the catheter and continue suction application for about 30 seconds.
options.B: Preoxygenate before suctioning and limit each suction application to a maximum of 15 seconds.
options.C: Instill normal saline before every pass and use deep suction routinely for secretion removal.
options.D: Perform suction on a fixed schedule even when assessment shows no clinical indication.

rationale: The active 2022 AARC Clinical Practice Guideline for Artificial Airway Suctioning recommends preoxygenation before suctioning in adult patients and limiting suction application to a maximum of 15 seconds per suctioning procedure. The guideline also generally advises against normal-saline instillation, recommends deep suction only when shallow suction is ineffective, and supports suctioning based on clinical indications rather than unnecessary routine practice. Therefore B is correct. A prolongs suction exposure, C combines two practices the guideline does not recommend routinely, and D ignores indication-based assessment.
educational_objective: Perform artificial-airway suctioning with preoxygenation and brief suction applications of no more than 15 seconds while avoiding routine saline instillation, unnecessary deep suction, and non-indicated scheduled suctioning.
source_document_title: AARC Clinical Practice Guidelines: Artificial Airway Suctioning
source_version_date: Respiratory Care 2022;67(2):258-271; remains listed as active AARC evidence-based CPG in 2026
source_locator: Guideline recommendations: preoxygenation before suctioning in pediatric/adult patients; normal saline generally avoided; suction maximum 15 seconds per procedure; deep suction only when shallow suction is ineffective. AARC current Clinical Practice Guidelines page lists Artificial Airway Suctioning (2022) under active Evidence-Based CPGs.
source_claim_supported: Adult artificial-airway suctioning should include preoxygenation and suction application no longer than 15 seconds; routine saline and deep suction are discouraged and suction should be clinically indicated.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation: manage acute respiratory alterations, perform emergency/airway care procedures, monitor response to interventions, and prevent treatment-related complications.

source_original.stem: A nurse is suctioning an adult client through an artificial airway. Which technique is consistent with current AARC guidance?

options.A: Apply suction while advancing the catheter and continue the suction application for about 30 seconds.
options.B: Preoxygenate as indicated and limit each suction application to no more than about 15 seconds.
options.C: Instill normal saline before every pass and use deep suction routinely for secretion removal.
options.D: Perform suction on a fixed schedule even when assessment shows no clinical indication.

source_original.rationale: AARC recommends preoxygenation as indicated and limiting suction application to a maximum of 15 seconds. It generally advises against routine saline instillation, favors suctioning when indicated rather than on a fixed schedule, and reserves deep suctioning for cases in which shallow suction is ineffective. Option B is correct.
source_original.source_detail: Artificial Airway Suctioning guideline recommendations: suction only when indicated; preoxygenate adult/pediatric patients as appropriate; use sterile technique for open suctioning; generally avoid routine saline; limit suction application to a maximum of 15 seconds; use deep suction only if shallow suction is ineffective. 2022 AARC Artificial Airway Suctioning guideline remains an active evidence-based guideline on the AARC site; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, emergency response and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the artificial-airway suction construct and key B. Tightened the wording to the AARC maximum-15-second recommendation, preserved preoxygenation, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium because the final item tests a direct procedural guideline bundle.

audit_findings.source_authority: AARC evidence-based CPG; official NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: AARC 2022 guideline remains listed among active evidence-based CPGs in 2026; live-rechecked 2026-08-16
audit_findings.exact_locator: PubMed abstract recommendations 4, 5, 8, 9; AARC active CPG listing
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item uses explicit AARC recommendations and does not add unsupported suction pressures, catheter sizes, or number of passes.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because suction application should not last 30 seconds and suction is not applied continuously while advancing.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because routine saline is generally avoided and deep suction is reserved for shallow-suction failure.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because suction should be driven by clinical indications rather than unnecessary fixed scheduling.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B contains two affirmative AARC-supported techniques without a contradictory unsafe practice.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives describe procedural suctioning strategies and are comparable in structure.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation — airway intervention and complication prevention.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked active AARC listing, PubMed guideline recommendations, all options, rationale, objective, NCSBN mapping, ambiguity and cueing. B remained uniquely correct.
